title: Mineral and Energy Belts of the World

cards.h: Resources explain trade, war and diplomacy
cards.b:
Where minerals lie shapes industry, shipping and politics. Questions ask you to name the belts, explain why they are where they are, and link to geopolitics such as oil, rare earths and critical minerals. Think in belts, not lists.

Resource geography is also about control: who owns the mine, who owns the port and who sets the price. Keep this three-part lens for every belt below.

Minerals form with rock history. Ancient shields (Canadian, Scandinavian, Australian, African, Indian) hold iron, gold, nickel and copper. Young fold mountains (Andes, Rockies) hold copper, tin, silver. Sedimentary basins hold coal, oil and gas. Volcanic belts hold sulphur and geothermal heat.

Most coal is in the northern hemisphere. Largest producers: China, India, Indonesia, USA, Australia. Key regions: Appalachians (USA), Ruhr and Silesia (Europe), Donbas (Ukraine), Kuznetsk (Russia), Shanxi (China), Queensland and New South Wales (Australia), Damodar valley (India). Australia and Indonesia lead exports.

Remember that coal use is shifting. China and India burn most of it, and global demand is expected to plateau as renewable energy grows, though Indonesia and India still expand output.

The Persian Gulf basin holds over half of proven reserves: Saudi Arabia, Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, UAE. Others: Russia (West Siberia), USA (Texas, Gulf of Mexico, Permian), Venezuela (Orinoco heavy oil, the largest reserves), Canada (Alberta oil sands), Nigeria, Libya and the North Sea. OPEC (1960, Baghdad, now in Vienna) coordinates supply; OPEC+ includes Russia.

Leading countries: Australia (Pilbara, Western Australia), Brazil (Carajas, Minas Gerais), China, India, Russia. Iron ore is exported from Port Hedland and Tubarao. Manganese: South Africa, Gabon, Australia. Nickel: Indonesia, Philippines, Russia. Chromium: South Africa, Kazakhstan.

Australia and Brazil together supply most seaborne iron ore. Because steel plants in China, Japan and Korea buy it, ore prices and shipping costs link directly with Asian industry.

Copper: the Andean belt, Chile (Chuquicamata, Escondida), Peru, plus the Congo-Zambia Copperbelt. Bauxite: Australia, Guinea, Brazil, Jamaica. Gold: Witwatersrand (South Africa), China, Australia, Russia, Canada. Tin: the Malay and Indonesian belt. Diamond: Russia, Botswana, DR Congo.

Zambia and the DR Congo share the Central African Copperbelt. Cobalt is mined as a by-product of copper and nickel, so these metals are tied together by geology as well as demand.

Needed for batteries, magnets and chips: lithium (the 'lithium triangle': Argentina, Bolivia, Chile; plus Australia), cobalt (DR Congo about 70 percent), rare earths (China dominates mining and over 85 percent of refining), graphite (China), nickel (Indonesia). Because the supply is concentrated, countries have started minerals diplomacy.

Richard Auty (1993) coined the 'resource curse': mineral-rich states often grow slowly because of corruption, conflict and currency overvaluation (Dutch disease). Examples: Nigeria, DR Congo, Venezuela. Counter-examples: Norway built a sovereign wealth fund; Botswana managed diamonds well. The difference lies in institutions.

The 2010 dispute between China and Japan on rare-earth exports, and the later US-China trade rows, showed how supply concentration can become a political weapon.

India has coal, iron ore, bauxite and mica but imports most of its oil, lithium, cobalt, nickel and rare earths. It joined the Minerals Security Partnership (2023), set up KABIL (2019) for overseas assets in Argentina and Australia, and launched a National Critical Mineral Mission (2025). Compare with the world belts to explain priorities.

Likely questions: 'Distribution of major minerals and their geopolitics', 'Why are the Persian Gulf states so vital?', 'Critical minerals and India'.

  • Sketch a world map with belts and write two examples each.
  • Link supply concentration to risk.
  • Propose diversification: recycling, partnerships, domestic exploration.

Rare earths are not rare in the crust, but are costly to separate. The Chinese lead came from low-cost mining and heavy state backing, plus lax environmental rules in early decades.
